title: Ohm's law
body: V = I × R. Voltage (volts) pushes current (amps) through resistance (ohms). Double the voltage across a fixed resistor and the current doubles. Rearranged: I = V / R and R = V / I. It is the first tool for almost every circuit calculation.

title: Electrical power
body: P = V × I, and with Ohm's law P = I²R = V²/R. A resistor carrying 0.5 A with 10 Ω dissipates 0.5² × 10 = 2.5 W as heat, so a 1/4 W resistor would burn. Always check power ratings, not just resistance.

title: Series and parallel resistors
body: In series, resistances add: R = R1 + R2, and the same current flows through both. In parallel, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2, and the total is always smaller than the smallest one. Two equal resistors in parallel give half the value.

title: Kirchhoff's laws
body: Current law (KCL): currents into a node equal currents out, because charge is conserved. Voltage law (KVL): voltages around any closed loop sum to zero, because energy is conserved. With Ohm's law these let you solve any linear circuit.

title: The voltage divider
body: Two resistors in series split a voltage: Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2). With 12 V, R1 = 10 kΩ and R2 = 5 kΩ, Vout = 4 V. Dividers scale sensor signals for an ADC, but sag if the load draws significant current.

title: Capacitors and the RC time constant
body: A capacitor stores charge: Q = C × V. Charging through a resistor, it reaches about 63% of the supply after one time constant τ = R × C, and about 99% after 5τ. With 10 kΩ and 100 µF, τ = 1 second.

title: Inductors resist change
body: An inductor's voltage is V = L × di/dt: it opposes changes in current. Switch off current through a relay coil and di/dt is huge, so the coil produces a large voltage spike. That spike destroys transistors unless a flyback diode gives the current somewhere to go.

title: RMS voltage
body: AC voltage is quoted as RMS, the DC value that would heat a resistor equally. For a sine wave, peak = RMS × √2. Zimbabwe's 220 V, 50 Hz mains therefore peaks at about 311 V, which matters when choosing capacitor and diode voltage ratings.

title: Power factor
body: Motors and other inductive loads draw current that lags the voltage, so some current does no useful work. Power factor = real power (W) / apparent power (VA). A low power factor means bigger currents, hotter cables and utility penalties. Capacitor banks correct it.

title: Three-phase power
body: Three-phase supplies use three sine waves 120° apart. They deliver smooth, constant power and naturally create a rotating magnetic field for motors. Line-to-line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage: 230 V phases give about 400 V between lines.

title: The diode
body: A diode lets current flow one way. A silicon diode drops about 0.6–0.7 V when conducting; an LED drops 1.8–3.3 V depending on colour; a Schottky diode about 0.3 V. Reverse it and almost no current flows until breakdown.

title: The bridge rectifier
body: Four diodes arranged as a bridge steer both halves of an AC wave the same way, giving pulsing DC. A smoothing capacitor then fills the gaps. The output peaks two diode drops (about 1.4 V) below the AC peak.

title: Zener diodes
body: A Zener diode is designed to conduct in reverse at a precise voltage, such as 5.1 V. With a series resistor it holds a node near that voltage, making a simple reference or overvoltage clamp. For real power supplies, linear or switching regulators do better.

title: The BJT as a switch
body: A small base current controls a collector current up to about β times larger (β is often 100 or more). To use a BJT as a switch, drive the base hard enough to saturate it, so it drops only about 0.2 V and stays cool.

title: MOSFETs
body: A MOSFET is controlled by gate voltage, not current, so it takes almost no steady drive. Fully on, it acts like a small resistance, RDS(on), often a few milliohms. Choose a logic-level MOSFET when driving it straight from a 3.3 V or 5 V microcontroller pin.

title: The flyback diode
body: Put a diode across every relay coil, solenoid or DC motor, pointing against the supply. When the switch opens, the coil's collapsing field drives current round through the diode instead of creating a spike of hundreds of volts across your transistor.

title: Op-amp golden rules
body: With negative feedback, an ideal op-amp obeys two rules: no current flows into the inputs, and the output does whatever it takes to make both inputs equal. These two rules let you analyse amplifiers, filters and buffers in a few lines.

title: Inverting and non-inverting gain
body: Inverting amplifier: gain = −Rf / Rin. Non-inverting amplifier: gain = 1 + Rf / Rin. With Rf = 100 kΩ and Rin = 10 kΩ, those are −10 and 11. The non-inverting version also has very high input impedance, so it barely loads the source.

title: Pulse-width modulation
body: PWM switches a supply fully on and off very fast and varies the on-time fraction, the duty cycle. 30% duty on 12 V delivers an average of 3.6 V to a motor or LED. Because the switch is either fully on or off, little power is wasted as heat.

title: The buck converter
body: A buck converter steps DC down efficiently: a switch chops the input, and an inductor plus capacitor smooth it. Ideally Vout = D × Vin, where D is the duty cycle. Efficiencies above 90% are normal, compared with a linear regulator that burns the difference as heat.

title: Induction motor speed
body: Synchronous speed = 120 × f / p, with f the supply frequency and p the number of poles. A 4-pole motor on 50 Hz has a synchronous speed of 1500 rpm; the rotor runs slightly slower, about 1450 rpm, because slip is needed to induce rotor current.

title: Variable frequency drives
body: A VFD rectifies mains to DC, then uses IGBTs and PWM to build new AC at any frequency. Motor speed follows frequency, so pumps and fans can slow down instead of being throttled. Since fan power scales with speed cubed, running 20% slower saves about half the energy.

title: The 4–20 mA current loop
body: Industrial sensors often send readings as a current between 4 and 20 mA. Current is the same all round the loop, so long cables and resistance don't distort it. The 'live zero' at 4 mA means 0 mA signals a broken wire rather than a zero reading.

title: Thermocouples
body: Join two different metals and the junction produces a small voltage that depends on temperature (the Seebeck effect). A type K thermocouple gives about 41 µV per °C and works to over 1000 °C. The reading needs cold-junction compensation and careful amplification.

title: PID control
body: A PID controller drives an error to zero using three terms. Proportional reacts to the present error, integral removes steady offset by adding up past error, and derivative damps overshoot by reacting to how fast the error changes. Most industrial loops are PI.

title: The PLC scan cycle
body: A PLC repeats one loop every few milliseconds: read all inputs, run the program (often ladder logic) top to bottom, then write all outputs. Because outputs update only at the end of each scan, very short input pulses can be missed unless they use fast inputs or interrupts.

title: ADC resolution
body: An n-bit analogue-to-digital converter splits its range into 2^n steps. A 12-bit ADC on 0–3.3 V has 4096 steps of about 0.8 mV. Sampling must also be fast enough: at least twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist), or fake low frequencies appear.

title: Earth leakage protection
body: A residual-current device (RCD) compares the current going out on live with the current returning on neutral. If more than about 30 mA goes missing, perhaps through a person to earth, it trips in a fraction of a second. Fuses and breakers protect cables; RCDs protect people.

title: Where Zimbabwe's power comes from
body: Most of Zimbabwe's electricity comes from the Kariba South hydro station and the coal-fired Hwange power station. When drought lowers Lake Kariba, hydro output must be cut, one of the main causes of load-shedding, which is why solar and grid expansion matter.

title: The transistor was born in 1947
body: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley built the first working transistor at Bell Labs in 1947 and shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. It replaced fragile, power-hungry vacuum tubes and made modern electronics possible.

title: Resistors in parallel
body: Circuit check.
statement: Two 100 Ω resistors in parallel give 200 Ω
explanation: In parallel, equal resistors give half the value: 1/R = 1/100 + 1/100, so R = 50 Ω. In series they would give 200 Ω.

title: Transformer ratio
body: Machines check.
statement: A 10:1 step-down transformer turns 220 V into 22 V
explanation: Voltage scales with the turns ratio: 220 V ÷ 10 = 22 V. Current scales the other way, ideally 10 times larger.

title: Peak of the mains
body: AC check.
statement: 220 V RMS mains peaks at about 311 V

title: Charging a capacitor
body: RC check.
statement: A capacitor is fully charged after one time constant
explanation: After one time constant it reaches about 63%. It takes about five time constants to reach 99%.

title: Heater current
body: Power check.
statement: A 2 kW heater on 230 V draws about 8.7 A
explanation: I = P / V = 2000 / 230 ≈ 8.7 A, so it needs a circuit rated above that, typically 10 A or more.
